summary: Defines a MIB that enables policy-based monitoring and management of SNMP infrastructures, including a scripting capability.

eli5.summary: Instead of giving instructions to each machine one by one, you write rules once and let the machines follow them.

questions: what is the policy based management mib
how do snmp policy scripts work
what is a precedence group in policy based management
subtitle: Rules instead of device-by-device commands: an SNMP MIB that lets devices run small policy scripts on their own.

tldr.problem: Large networks cannot be managed well one device at a time, where orders of magnitude more decisions, and mistakes, get made. Operators want to state a business policy once and have it apply to every matching element in every vendor's gear.
tldr.mechanism: The Policy Based Management MIB defines SNMP tables for installing policies in the form if (policyCondition) then (policyAction), written in a small C-like language called PolicyScript. An execution environment on or near the device discovers elements, runs the condition on each, and runs the action where it matches.
tldr.outcome: It adds roles, capabilities and schedules so policies can depend on things not otherwise stored on devices, and it ties script access to the credentials of whoever installed them. It is a Proposed Standard.

facts.label: Minimum scratchpad variables
facts.value: 50 Global, 5 per policy, 5 per policy-element pair

today: RFC 4011 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC itself points to RFC 3512 for configuration management practices that may help those using policy-based configuration.

sections.title: Managing by Policy, Not by Device
sections.content:
Large IT organizations try to configure the network as a whole by describing high-level business policies, rather than managing device by device. The RFC gives examples such as: all routers will run code version 6.2, on-site contractors only connect to ports with special security restrictions, or all ports whose customers paid for premium service get special forwarding. Each of these could mean an action applied to hundreds of thousands of variables.

To automate this, customers need software tools and standard protocols that work on all devices regardless of vendor. RFC 4011 defines SNMP managed objects used to distribute policies in a common form throughout the network. It is a MIB module that follows SMIv2, as described in RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580, and it is part of the Internet-Standard Management Framework overviewed in RFC 3410.
sections.eli5: Telling a thousand machines the same thing one at a time is slow and easy to get wrong. A single rule that every machine reads for itself is much easier.

sections.title: Conditions, Actions and Elements
sections.content:
Policies take the normal form if (policyCondition) then (policyAction). A policyCondition is a script that yields a boolean saying whether an element belongs to the set to act on. A policyAction is an operation performed on that element. Conceptually, for each element where the condition returns true, the action is executed on it.

An element is an instance of a physical or logical entity, embodied by a group of related MIB variables, such as all the variables for interface 7. Elements can also model circuits, CPUs, queues, processes and systems. Each unique pairing of a policy and an element is an execution context, and within it the phrase this element refers to the associated element.

Policies are normally executed on or near the managed devices, where element characteristics are easy to inspect. A management station distributes the policies, and the pmPolicyTable holds a policy on the device. A policy manager can manage elements on its own system or on other systems.
sections.eli5: A policy is an 'if this, then that' rule. The 'if' part checks one thing, such as one network port. The 'then' part does something to it only when the check says yes.

sections.title: Roles, Capabilities, Time and the Policy Manager
sections.content:
Many useful characteristics are not in any MIB, so this document adds three missing areas: roles, capabilities and time.

A role is an administratively specified characteristic of an element, such as political (executive, outside-contractor), financial or legal (paid, gold, trial), geographical (California, Headquarters) or architectural (backup, trunk). Roles are human-defined strings assigned through the role table, and several can be assigned to one element. They are meant for information not available in MIB objects, since policy code can read those directly. When a new role appears, a pmNewRoleNotification lets the management station install policies that use it.

The capabilities tables tell a management station what capabilities exist on a system, with a pmNewCapabilityNotification for new ones. For time, a schedule table controls when a policy is ready and when it is dormant, for regular periods (Monday to Friday, 9 to 5) or ad hoc ones.

The policy manager groups its objects into policy download and control (pmPolicyTable, pmElementTypeRegTable, pmSchedTable), policy environment control (pmRoleTable, capabilities tables) and policy monitoring (tracking tables, pmDebuggingTable), plus an execution environment with a policy scheduler, the language and a function library.
sections.eli5: Some facts a rule needs are not written anywhere on the machine, like 'this port belongs to a gold customer'. Roles are sticky labels people attach, and schedules say when each rule is switched on.

sections.title: How Policies Run
sections.content:
Execution has three steps in order: element discovery, element filtering and policy enforcement.

Discovery. The element type registration table lists what element types the system manages and lets managers add more. A type is registered by giving the OID of an SNMP object without the instance, and each instance under it is a distinct element. A special element type 0.0 is the system element, always present, useful for policies about the system itself or about scalar objects. Agents may discover elements by scanning internal data structures or by being told asynchronously, instead of polling.

Filtering. A policy is only ready if it is valid and either has no schedule (pmPolicySchedule is zero) or is linked to a schedule group with an active entry. The condition is called once per element, with the element name as its only argument, and runs to completion. If it returns non-zero, the action runs for that element. If a run-time exception (RTE) occurs, the element is simply not matched.

Enforcement. The action is called with the element name as its only argument. No state is kept between invocations except through library functions such as the scratchpad and SNMP functions. A new match runs the action immediately; later checks keep it within the policy's maximum latency.

Policies can be put in a precedence group: for each element, only the matching ready policy with the highest precedence is active. A gold-interface policy, for example, will win over a default bronze policy on gold ports.
sections.eli5: The device first finds all its parts, then asks the rule's 'if' question about each one, and finally does the 'then' part only to the parts that said yes. If two rules fit, the more important one wins.

sections.title: The PolicyScript Language
sections.content:
Conditions and actions are written in PolicyScript, a small interpreted language meant to look familiar to C and Perl programmers. It is defined formally as a subset of ISO C++ using an EBNF grammar. Function definitions, pointers, structures, enums, typedefs, floating point and pre-processor features (except comments) are not available. All variables in a script share one scope, and the code must be ASCII.

There is one data class, var, modeled on ECMAScript, which holds either a string (a finite sequence of 8-bit values, binary-safe) or an integer in the range -2^63 to 2^64-1. Positive overflow wraps modulo 2^64, integer division rounds toward zero, and automatic type conversion applies. Reserved C words such as struct and switch cannot be used.

A script ends with return or by reaching its end; the value is converted to a boolean, and falling off the end returns zero. For a condition, one means run the action; for an action, the value is ignored. A syntax error, an unknown identifier, a wrong argument count or exceeding local limits causes an RTE.

To address 'this element', a token such as $0 inside a string expands to the nth subidentifier of the element's index ($n accepts 0 to 128), and $* expands to the whole index. The functions ec() and ev() give the count and the values of the index components.
sections.eli5: PolicyScript is a tiny programming language that borrows the look of C. It can only do small jobs, which keeps it simple enough for any device to run.

sections.title: Function Libraries and the Schedule Table
sections.content:
Built-in functions are grouped into libraries, the unit of conformance. The required pmBaseFunctionLibrary has SNMP functions, policy functions, utility functions and general functions, and an implementation must provide all of them. A library's name is registered in the role table for the system element 0.0, so a script can test for it with roleMatch.

The SNMP functions come in two sets: simple convenience functions (getVar, exists, setVar, searchColumn, setRowStatus, createRow, counterRate) and general functions for building nearly any SNMP message, including multiple varbinds and notifications. The policy functions include elementName, roleMatch, signalError, defer, fail and getParameters. defer and fail let a failing policy fall through to the next-highest precedence policy.

The scratchpad functions store a named value with Global, Policy or PolicyElement scope, volatile or non-volatile. Implementations must support at least 50 Global variables, 5 Policy variables per policy and 5 PolicyElement variables per policy-element pair. A separate International String Library works on UTF-8 and defines a stringprep profile.

The schedule table adapts the policyTimePeriodCondition class of RFC 3060 and uses iCalendar formats. A policy points to a group of schedules and is ready when any of them is active. A schedule is active when it matches all of its time period, month, day, weekday and time of day settings, with bits within one object ORed together.
sections.eli5: The language comes with a toolbox of ready-made helpers for reading and changing settings, remembering things between runs, and checking the clock, so each rule stays short.

sections.title: Security of Policy Scripts
sections.content:
No object in this MIB discloses sensitive information when read. However, with the exception of pmPolicyDescription, pmPolicyDebugging, pmElementTypeRegDescription and pmSchedDescr, every read-write or read-create object should be treated as sensitive, because someone who could change them could make the system use the stored credentials of an authorized user for harmful operations.

An implementation must apply access control when scripts perform SNMP operations. It must record the securityModel, securityName and securityLevel of the last entity to modify each policy's pmPolicyAdminStatus, and use them as input to isAccessAllowed from RFC 3411. Unless all users with write access to the policy tables have equivalent access to the managed system, one user could gain another's privileges, so policies of different users should be protected from each other, for example by keeping each user's policies in one pmPolicyAdminGroup.

The RFC recommends SNMPv3 with its cryptographic security and says deploying versions before SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED. It also advises managers to install any security-related policy that might ever be needed, even if a role or capability it depends on does not exist yet, to avoid a delay that could expose the network.
sections.eli5: A rule runs with the permissions of the person who last switched it on. So the device must make sure that nobody can slip in a rule that borrows someone else's keys.

viz.caption: THE THREE STEPS OF POLICY EXECUTION (RFC 4011, SECTION 4)

items.title: 1. Element discovery
items.text: Find the elements of each registered type, plus the system element 0.0.

items.title: 2. Element filtering
items.text: If the policy is ready, run its condition once per element.

items.title: 3. Policy enforcement
items.text: Run the action on every element whose condition returned non-zero.
